notes.meaning: Asher's border turned east toward Beth-dagon, touched Zebulun and the Valley of Iphtah-el, and ran north past Cabul on the left. In ancient Hebrew directions, being on the left meant being to the north, because people faced east toward the sunrise. Beth-dagon had been named for the Canaanite false god Dagon, showing how widespread idol worship was in Canaan before Israel arrived.

The border continued north through towns like Kanah all the way to Greater Sidon on the Mediterranean coast. Sidon was an ancient and wealthy Phoenician seaport known across the region. God assigned this area to Asher, but the Israelites never fully drove out the Sidonians or took over their city.

The boundary looped south toward Ramah and reached the fortified city of Tyre before turning to the Mediterranean Sea near Achzib. Tyre was a famous Phoenician stronghold, and its mainland defenses were already powerful in Joshua's day. Like Sidon, Tyre remained outside Israelite control throughout this period.

The description finishes Asher's northern territory by listing Ummah, Aphek, and Rehob, counting twenty-two cities with their surrounding villages. Aphek later served as a battleground during Israel's history with neighboring kingdoms. The total count includes only the main towns belonging strictly to Asher, leaving out border fortresses like Tyre and Sidon.

This summary confirms that the rich coastal plain and western hills were the official homeland for the clans of Asher. God gave this fertile ground as a generous gift, fulfilling earlier blessings that Asher would enjoy good food and wealth. Even with such a bountiful portion, the tribe still had to step out in faith and drive out the remaining Canaanites.

The sixth lot chosen at Shiloh went to the clans of the tribe of Naphtali. God assigned their land after Asher and Zebulun, placing them in eastern Galilee. Even though Dan was the older brother by birth, God chose to call Naphtali's lot first, showing that His gifts do not depend on human rank.

Naphtali's northern boundary began at Heleph near the great sacred oak of Zaanannim and ended eastward at the Jordan River. Zaanannim stood near Kedesh, high in the hills above the upper Jordan valley. This description traces how Naphtali's northern border swept all the way to the main water source of the land.

The southern border turned west toward Aznoth-tabor and touched Zebulun on the south, Asher on the west, and the Jordan on the east. The phrase mentioning Judah at the Jordan points to river communication or family settlements of Judah across the river through Jair. Naphtali was surrounded by sister tribes who could help defend the northern frontier.

Naphtali received several strongly fortified cities, including Hammath, Rakkath, and Chinnereth along the Sea of Galilee. Chinnereth was the ancient town that gave its name to the entire lake, later known as Gennesaret or Galilee. These walled towns protected the vital trade routes passing through northern Israel.

The list of Naphtali's fortified towns continues with Adamah, Ramah, and Hazor, followed by Kedesh, Edrei, and En-hazor. Hazor had been the major Canaanite royal center in the north until Joshua burned it, while Kedesh later served as a safe city of refuge. These strong positions gave Naphtali natural fortresses in the rugged upper hill country.

The final group of Naphtali's fortified towns includes Iron, Migdal-el, Horem, Beth-anath, and Beth-shemesh, bringing the total to nineteen walled cities plus their surrounding farming villages. Several of these towns originally housed Canaanite shrines, such as Beth-shemesh, which means house of the sun. God gave these former strongholds of pagan worship to His people to live in peacefully.

This conclusion wraps up the inheritance allotted to all the families of Naphtali with their towns and outlying villages. Their territory gave them lovely hills, fertile valleys, and a direct view over the Sea of Galilee. Hundreds of years later, Jesus spent much of His earthly ministry teaching and healing right in this region.

The seventh and final tribal lot came out for the clans of Dan. Dan was one of the largest tribes in Israel during the wilderness journey, yet their assigned allotment came last. God placed them in a strategic buffer zone between the mountain tribes and the powerful Philistine cities along the Mediterranean coast.

Dan's inheritance is outlined by towns rather than boundary lines, beginning with Zorah, Eshtaol, Ir-shemesh, Shaalabbin, and Aijalon. Several of these towns had previously been counted with Judah's large territory and were now reassigned to Dan. Aijalon became famous as the valley where the moon stood still during Joshua's battle against the Amorite kings.

The list of Danite towns continues with Elon, Timnah, Ekron, Eltekeh, Gibbethon, and Baalath. Ekron was one of the five major Philistine city-states, and Israel struggled for generations to hold this coastal borderland. Even though God marked out these cities for Dan, powerful enemies kept the Danites from settling many of them right away.

Dan's region extended toward the Mediterranean Sea, taking in Jehud, Bene-berak, Gath-rimmon, and the territory right across from the harbor of Joppa. Joppa was the main natural seaport along the coast of central Israel, where timber was later brought to build the temple. Dan received fertile land close to trade paths, but living next to the sea meant facing constant pressure from Philistine neighbors.

When the Amorites and Philistines pushed the Danites out of their allotted valleys, part of the tribe marched far to the north and captured the remote city of Leshem. They took the city by the sword, settled there, and renamed it Dan in honor of their tribal forefather. This northern conquest gave Israel its famous boundary marker, stretching from Dan in the far north to Beersheba in the south.

A summary concludes the record of Dan's inheritance, counting all the cities and farming hamlets assigned to their families. The Bible includes both their original southern towns and their northern colony so that the entire story of Dan's settlements is kept together. God faithfully designated a full portion for Dan, even when the tribe faced hardship occupying it.

After every single tribe had received its allotted land, the leaders and people of Israel gave Joshua his own personal inheritance among them. Joshua showed great humility and selflessness by making sure every family had a home before he asked for anything himself. A godly leader seeks the good of others before looking after his own comfort.

In keeping with the Lord's command, the people gave Joshua the city he requested, Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim. He did not ask for a rich palace or an easy valley, but chose a rugged mountain town in his own tribe, which he repaired and lived in. Joshua spent his remaining years faithfully serving God in the quiet city he helped rebuild.

Eleazar the high priest, Joshua, and the tribal heads formally finished dividing the entire land by lot before the Lord at the entrance of the Tabernacle in Shiloh. Doing this sacred work directly before God ensured that the outcome came from His hand and that all the tribes accepted their shares without dispute. God proved entirely true to His promise, giving Israel the homeland He had sworn to Abraham centuries before.
